name: Daffy's Elixir

lead: Daffy's Elixir, also sold as Elixir Salutis, was an English proprietary medicine made by steeping senna and other plant drugs in spirits. Marketed from the later 1600s into the 1900s, it was advertised as a universal remedy for ailments from colic to gout, and it worked as a purgative cordial.

Its appeal as a wellness product fit the period idea that purging cleared the body and supported health and a good complexion, though sources describe its listed uses as advertising claims rather than tested outcomes. It is mainly remembered historically, in literature and in slang where 'daffy' meant gin.

paras: It was taken by the spoonful or dose as a drink, and was also given to infants and to horses in the period. Recipes varied by maker and generally steeped senna, with items such as aniseed, fennel, rhubarb and liquorice, in aqua vitae or brandy.

Chemical analysis described in historical accounts shows it was a laxative made mostly of alcohol. Use in infants and animals was criticised at the time, including in early veterinary manuals. It is not a currently marketed product.

angle.text: Historically taken as a purging health cordial; it was sold as a general remedy rather than as a cosmetic, and any appearance benefit rests on period beliefs about cleansing.

lead: Daffy's Elixir, also called Elixir Salutis, was an English proprietary medicine made by steeping plant drugs, almost always including senna, in distilled spirit [1]. It was made and widely used from the later seventeenth century into the twentieth in England, North America and parts of Europe [1].

Its link to personal appearance is through the era's health culture: it was advertised as a general remedy and cleansing purge, and users took it as a tonic. The listed uses were marketing claims, and no modern trial has examined it. Its legacy is historical, in the account books and bottles that document the early patent-medicine trade, in slang where 'daffy' meant gin, and in novels by Dickens and others [1][2].

paras: The remedy is attributed to Thomas Daffy, a Leicestershire clergyman who died in 1680, though its authorship is uncertain; Anthony Daffy, a London cordwainer who styled himself a student in medicine, publicised it in pamphlets from 1673 [1][2]. His account book records shipments to provincial agents and to customers in Ireland, the Netherlands, France, the Caribbean and New England [1]. Copies of the recipe circulated, and in the early 1720s a version without Daffy's name entered the pharmacopoeias of the Royal College of Physicians and of Edinburgh [1].

An early recipe for True Daffy from 1700 lists aniseed, brandy, cochineal, elecampane, fennel seed, jalap, manna, parsley seed, raisin, rhubarb, saffron, senna and Spanish liquorice [2]. An early nineteenth-century advertisement listed uses including convulsions, consumption, digestive problems, gout, rheumatism, colic, dropsy, scurvy, worms and rickets [2]. Counterfeiters were reported to use inferior alcohol in place of brandy [2].

About 1775 William and Cluer Dicey and Company produced it and claimed sole rights, although there was no patent; it later passed to Sutton and Company, which still made it in 1910 [1][2]. A statute of 1812 taxed it by name [1]. Dickens (Oliver Twist), Thackeray, Trollope and Pynchon mention it [2]. 'Daffy' became slang for gin, and in Oliver Twist a parish nurse gives gin as the infants' Daffy [1].
